title: Operating System Dual Mode Operation & Architecture
description: Analyze how CPU hardware prevents user programs from halting the machine or modifying kernel memory through mode bit and timer interrupts.
problemStatement: Explain the transition between User Mode and Kernel Mode. What triggers the switch from User to Kernel mode, and what instruction transitions back? Why must the timer interrupt be privileged?
sampleAnswer: Transitions to kernel mode occur via interrupts, exceptions, or software trap instructions (system calls). The hardware switches the mode bit to 0 (kernel mode), executes the kernel vector handler, and resumes user code with an 'RTI' (Return from Interrupt) or 'sysret' instruction which resets the mode bit to 1 (user mode). The timer interrupt ensures the OS retains control of the CPU; if user code could modify the timer, a malicious loop could monopolize the machine indefinitely.

title: System Call Tracing: File Copy Operation
description: Trace the exact sequence of system calls executed when copying a file from source to destination.
problemStatement: List the essential system calls in order for a command line utility `cp src.txt dest.txt` on a POSIX system. What error checks are required at each stage?
sampleAnswer:
1. `open('src.txt', O_RDONLY)` — Check if source exists and is readable.
2. `open('dest.txt', O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0644)` — Check if destination can be created/written.
3. Loop `read(fd_src, buffer, BUF_SIZE)` and `write(fd_dest, buffer, bytes_read)` until `read` returns 0 (EOF).
4. `close(fd_src)` and `close(fd_dest)`.
Error checking: Validate return values != -1 at each step; handle partial writes where `bytes_written < bytes_read`.

title: Process State Transitions & PCB Analysis
description: Model the exact fields in a Process Control Block and diagnose invalid state transitions.
problemStatement: Can a process transition directly from Waiting state to Running state in a uniprocessor operating system? Explain why or why not, detailing the role of the Ready queue.
sampleAnswer: No. A process in the Waiting state is waiting for an asynchronous event (e.g., disk I/O, network packet, timer). When the event occurs, an interrupt handler signals completion and moves the process to the Ready state. The CPU is currently executing another process (or the kernel). The newly readied process must wait its turn in the Ready queue until the short-term CPU scheduler dispatches it to the Running state.

title: fork() System Call Tree & Execution Count
description: Calculate the exact number of processes created by consecutive fork calls.
sampleAnswer:
Initial: 1 process (P0).
1. fork(): P0 forks P1 (total 2 processes).
2. if (fork() == 0): Both P0 and P1 execute this fork. P0 creates child P2 (in P0, fork() returns PID > 0, so if condition is false). P1 creates child P3 (in P1, fork() returns PID > 0, so if condition is false). For P2 and P3, fork() returns 0, so they enter the if block!
3. Inside if block: P2 forks P4, P3 forks P5.
Total processes created = 6 processes (P0, P1, P2, P3, P4, P5).
All 6 processes reach `printf("PRIME\n")`.
Output: 'PRIME' is printed 6 times.

title: FCFS and SJF CPU Scheduling Numerical
description: Calculate Turnaround Time and Waiting Time for FCFS and SJF (non-preemptive).
problemStatement:
Four processes arrive as follows:
P1: Arrival = 0, Burst = 8
P2: Arrival = 1, Burst = 4
P3: Arrival = 2, Burst = 9
P4: Arrival = 3, Burst = 5
Compute the average turnaround time and average waiting time for: (a) FCFS, (b) SJF non-preemptive.
sampleAnswer:
Part (a) FCFS:
Gantt Chart: | P1 (0-8) | P2 (8-12) | P3 (12-21) | P4 (21-26) |
CT: P1=8, P2=12, P3=21, P4=26
TAT (CT - AT): P1=8, P2=11, P3=19, P4=23. Avg TAT = 61 / 4 = 15.25 ms
WT (TAT - BT): P1=0, P2=7, P3=10, P4=18. Avg WT = 35 / 4 = 8.75 ms

Part (b) SJF Non-Preemptive:
At t=0: Only P1 is present -> runs 0 to 8.
At t=8: P2(BT=4), P3(BT=9), P4(BT=5) are ready. Shortest is P2(4) -> runs 8 to 12.
At t=12: P4(5) vs P3(9) -> P4 runs 12 to 17.
At t=17: P3 runs 17 to 26.
Gantt: | P1 (0-8) | P2 (8-12) | P4 (12-17) | P3 (17-26) |
CT: P1=8, P2=12, P4=17, P3=26
TAT: P1=8, P2=11, P4=14, P3=24. Avg TAT = 57 / 4 = 14.25 ms
WT: P1=0, P2=7, P4=9, P3=15. Avg WT = 31 / 4 = 7.75 ms

title: Round Robin & SRTF Preemptive Scheduling
description: Simulate preemptive CPU scheduling with time quantum and remaining burst times.
problemStatement:
Given processes with AT and BT:
P1: AT=0, BT=5
P2: AT=1, BT=3
P3: AT=2, BT=8
P4: AT=3, BT=6
Simulate Round Robin with Time Quantum q = 2 ms. Construct the ready queue state at each context switch and find the average waiting time.
sampleAnswer:
Timeline (q=2):
t=0: P1 arrives. Runs [0, 2], remaining BT=3. At t=1 P2 arrives, at t=2 P3 arrives. Ready queue: [P2, P3, P1].
t=2: P2 runs [2, 4], remaining BT=1. At t=3 P4 arrives. Ready queue: [P3, P1, P4, P2].
t=4: P3 runs [4, 6], remaining BT=6. Ready queue: [P1, P4, P2, P3].
t=6: P1 runs [6, 8], remaining BT=1. Ready queue: [P4, P2, P3, P1].
t=8: P4 runs [8, 10], remaining BT=4. Ready queue: [P2, P3, P1, P4].
t=10: P2 runs [10, 11] -> FINISHED at t=11! Ready queue: [P3, P1, P4].
t=11: P3 runs [11, 13], remaining BT=4. Ready queue: [P1, P4, P3].
t=13: P1 runs [13, 14] -> FINISHED at t=14! Ready queue: [P4, P3].
t=14: P4 runs [14, 16], remaining BT=2. Ready queue: [P3, P4].
t=16: P3 runs [16, 18], remaining BT=2. Ready queue: [P4, P3].
t=18: P4 runs [18, 20] -> FINISHED at t=20! Ready queue: [P3].
t=20: P3 runs [20, 22] -> FINISHED at t=22!

Completion Times:
P1: CT=14, TAT=14, WT = 14 - 5 = 9
P2: CT=11, TAT=10, WT = 10 - 3 = 7
P3: CT=22, TAT=20, WT = 20 - 8 = 12
P4: CT=20, TAT=17, WT = 17 - 6 = 11
Average Waiting Time = (9 + 7 + 12 + 11) / 4 = 39 / 4 = 9.75 ms.

title: Peterson's Algorithm Correctness & Hardware Locks
description: Prove mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting in Peterson's algorithm.
sampleAnswer:
If both lines are inverted:
P0 sets `turn = 1;`
P1 sets `turn = 0;`
P0 sets `flag[0] = true;`
P0 checks `while (flag[1] && turn == 1)`. Since P1 has not set `flag[1] = true` yet (or if P1 was delayed right before setting flag[1]), P0 sees `flag[1] == false` and enters CS.
Simultaneously, P1 resumes and sets `flag[1] = true`. P1 checks `while (flag[0] && turn == 0)`. Notice that `turn` was set to 0 by P1, but if P0 had overwritten it before, or due to interleaving: both processes can observe their condition as false and enter the critical section simultaneously, causing a complete failure of Mutual Exclusion!

title: Banker's Algorithm: Safe Sequence & Resource Request
description: Determine system safety and grant/deny resource requests.
problemStatement:
A system has 5 processes (P0-P4) and 3 resource types A (10 instances), B (5 instances), C (7 instances).
Allocation: P0=[0,1,0], P1=[2,0,0], P2=[3,0,2], P3=[2,1,1], P4=[0,0,2].
Max: P0=[7,5,3], P1=[3,2,2], P2=[9,0,2], P3=[2,2,2], P4=[4,3,3].
Total Allocated = [7, 2, 5]. Available = [3, 3, 2].
(a) Compute Need matrix.
(b) Is the system in a safe state? Find a safe sequence.
(c) If P1 requests [1, 0, 2], can it be granted immediately?
sampleAnswer:
Part (a) Need Matrix (Max - Allocation):
P0: [7, 4, 3]
P1: [1, 2, 2]
P2: [6, 0, 0]
P3: [0, 1, 1]
P4: [4, 3, 1]

Part (b) Safety check with Available = [3, 3, 2]:
- Can P0 run? Need [7,4,3] <= [3,3,2]? No.
- Can P1 run? Need [1,2,2] <= [3,3,2]? Yes! P1 finishes.
  New Work = Available + Alloc(P1) = [3,3,2] + [2,0,0] = [5, 3, 2].
- Can P3 run? Need [0,1,1] <= [5,3,2]? Yes! P3 finishes.
  New Work = [5,3,2] + [2,1,1] = [7, 4, 3].
- Can P4 run? Need [4,3,1] <= [7,4,3]? Yes! P4 finishes.
  New Work = [7,4,3] + [0,0,2] = [7, 4, 5].
- Can P0 run? Need [7,4,3] <= [7,4,5]? Yes! P0 finishes.
  New Work = [7,4,5] + [0,1,0] = [7, 5, 5].
- Can P2 run? Need [6,0,0] <= [7,5,5]? Yes! P2 finishes.
  New Work = [7,5,5] + [3,0,2] = [10, 5, 7].
All processes satisfied! Safe sequence: <P1, P3, P4, P0, P2> (or <P1, P3, P0, P2, P4>).
System is SAFE.

Part (c) Request by P1 = [1, 0, 2]:
1. Request [1,0,2] <= Need [1,2,2]? Yes.
2. Request [1,0,2] <= Available [3,3,2]? Yes.
Tentative state:
Available' = [3,3,2] - [1,0,2] = [2, 3, 0]
Alloc'(P1) = [2,0,0] + [1,0,2] = [3, 0, 2]
Need'(P1) = [1,2,2] - [1,0,2] = [0, 2, 0]
Now test safety with Available' = [2, 3, 0]:
Can P1 run? Need [0,2,0] <= [2,3,0]? Yes! P1 finishes.
Work = [2,3,0] + [3,0,2] = [5, 3, 2].
From here, system is identical to previous safe state! Thus, the request CAN be granted immediately.

title: Paging & Page Replacement: FIFO, LRU, Optimal & Belady
description: Compute page faults across FIFO, LRU, and Optimal algorithms on reference strings.
problemStatement:
Given reference string: `7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1` with 3 frames.
Compute total page faults for:
(a) FIFO
(b) LRU
(c) Optimal
Also explain Belady's Anomaly and provide an example string where frame size 4 produces more faults than frame size 3.
sampleAnswer:
3-frame analysis:
(a) FIFO produces 15 page faults.
(b) LRU produces 12 page faults.
(c) Optimal produces 9 page faults.

Belady's Anomaly:
In FIFO page replacement, increasing the number of page frames can unexpectedly result in an INCREASE in page faults (unlike stack algorithms like LRU/Optimal where the set of pages in k frames is always a subset of pages in k+1 frames).
Famous Example String: `1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5`
- With 3 frames: FIFO yields 9 page faults.
- With 4 frames: FIFO yields 10 page faults! (Faults increase by 1 despite 33% more memory).

title: Operating Systems Comprehensive Interview Synthesis
description: 25 high-frequency conceptual interview questions across Concurrency, Memory, Scheduling and Storage.
problemStatement:
Synthesize key tradeoffs:
1. Thread vs Process overhead and memory isolation.
2. Inode file allocation vs Windows FAT/NTFS.
3. Convoy effect in FCFS vs Starvation in SJF.
4. Spinlock vs Mutex sleep lock in uniprocessor vs multicore.
5. Copy-on-Write (COW) mechanism in fork().
sampleAnswer:
1. Processes have independent address spaces, page tables, file descriptor tables, and require MMU remapping (context switch flushes TLB entries). Threads share text, data, heap, and open files, having only their own stack, registers, and program counter, making context switching significantly faster.
2. Inodes support O(1) direct block access via direct pointers and scale to terabytes via indirect/triple indirect pointers, keeping metadata separated from file names. FAT maintains a table in RAM where file blocks form a linked list, which suffers from random access latency and fragmentation.
3. Convoy effect occurs when a CPU-bound process with large burst holds CPU, causing many short I/O-bound jobs to wait in Ready queue. SJF minimizes average waiting time but starves long processes indefinitely if short jobs keep arriving (solved by aging).
4. Spinlocks busy-wait in a while loop checking an atomic lock; on a uniprocessor, a spinlock is always wasteful because the holding thread cannot run until the spinning thread yields CPU. On multi-core systems, spinlocks are optimal for very short critical sections (< context switch cost).
5. In `fork()`, modern OSes do not duplicate the parent's physical memory pages. Instead, parent and child share the same physical frames marked as READ-ONLY. When either process attempts to write to a page, a Page Fault exception is triggered, the kernel intercepts it, allocates a new physical frame, copies the single page, marks it read-write, and resumes execution. This saves massive memory and CPU cycles when `exec()` is called shortly after.
